Obtain an expression for average power dissipated in a series LCR circuit.
solution:
Consider a series LCR circuit across which an alternating voltage \(e = e_0\sin\omega t\) is applied. The current lags or leads by a phase angle \(\phi\), so

\(i = i_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)\)

The instantaneous power is the product of the instantaneous voltage and current:

\(P = ei = e_0 i_0 \sin\omega t\,\sin(\omega t - \phi)\)

Using the identity \(2\sin A\sin B = \cos(A - B) - \cos(A + B)\),

\(P = \dfrac{e_0 i_0}{2}\left[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)\right]\)

The average power is this quantity averaged over one full cycle. The first term is a constant, so it averages to itself. The second term is a cosine of \(2\omega t\), and the average of a cosine over a complete cycle is zero:

\(\overline{\cos(2\omega t - \phi)} = 0\)

Hence

\(P_{av} = \dfrac{e_0 i_0}{2}\cos\phi\)

Writing the peak values in terms of the rms values, \(e_0 = \sqrt{2}\,e_{rms}\) and \(i_0 = \sqrt{2}\,i_{rms}\),

\(P_{av} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}e_{rms} \times \sqrt{2}i_{rms}}{2}\cos\phi\)

\(\therefore P_{av} = e_{rms}\,i_{rms}\cos\phi\)

The factor \(\cos\phi\) is called the **power factor** of the circuit, and \(\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z}\). Substituting,

\(P_{av} = e_{rms}i_{rms}\dfrac{R}{Z} = i_{rms}^{2}R\)

so all the power consumed is dissipated in the resistance alone. For a purely inductive or purely capacitive circuit \(\phi = 90^{\circ}\), the power factor is zero and the average power is zero, which is why such a circuit is called wattless.
